title: Settings (mobile)
about: The settings screen of a phone app: grouped lists of options the person can change.

items.t: Grouped list with short section titles (Account, Notifications, Privacy, About)
Most used first; rarely used in deeper screens
Search in settings when there are many
App settings in the app, not in the system Settings app (iOS)
Each row: name, current value, and a chevron or toggle
Toggles take effect at once, no Save needed
Choices with few options open a list with a tick
Short help text under rows that need it
Destructive rows (Log out, Delete account) at the bottom, styled red
Notifications by kind
Language, with Arabic and right-to-left layout
Appearance: system, light, dark
Privacy, data download and account deletion
App version and build at the bottom
Help, terms, privacy policy links
Changes saved on the device and synced to the account
Settings that need the system (notifications off, location off) link to the system settings page
Toggles read their state ("Dark mode, switch, on")
Large text: rows grow and wrap, values move under names
Rows at least 44 pt / 48 dp

title: Sign up (mobile)
about: Creating an account in a phone app or mobile site. Started from checklist.design's 8 items, checked 2026-11-19.

items.t: One line saying what you get, above the form
Try before signing up (guest mode) where the product allows it
Ask for an account at the moment it is needed (save, buy, post), not on first open
Intro slides skippable, few of them
Sign up and Log in easy to tell apart
Sign up with Apple, Google or a social account
If any third-party sign-in is offered on iPhone, also offer one that limits data to name and email and can hide the email (Sign in with Apple qualifies)
Phone number sign-up with a country-code picker (strong in the Gulf)
Passkey sign-up: email first, say a passkey is part of sign-up before the phone's prompt, keep a fallback
Same email from a social account links to the existing account, no dead end
Sign-up stays in the app, never sent out to the web browser
Only the fields needed (each extra one lowers completion)
Email field brings the email keyboard; phone brings the number pad
Password manager can fill and save (marked as new password and username)
Auto-capitalise and auto-correct off on email and username
Labels stay visible; hint text alone disappears when typing
Return key moves to the next field and sends on the last
Paste allowed everywhere, passwords and codes too
Spaces at the start and end trimmed
"Did you mean gmail.com?" on a typo
Name field accepts any name (Arabic, one word, hyphens)
No confirm-password field; a show/hide button instead
Length over symbols: no "must have a capital and a symbol" rules
Long passwords allowed (at least 64 characters)
Known leaked or common passwords refused, with a kind message
Rules shown up front and ticked as met; strength shown while typing
Each field checked when the person leaves it, not while typing
Error removed as soon as the field is fixed; a tick when it is right
Error next to the field, saying how to fix it
Errors never erase what was typed
No-connection state keeps what was typed and offers retry
Errors read aloud by screen readers
Helpful: "This email has an account" with Log in and Reset right there
Private: same answer whether the email exists or not, details sent by email
Terms and privacy accepted before the account is made, readable in the app
Marketing opt-in separate, off by default, as easy to withdraw
Age asked neutrally (type birth month and year, no "I am over 12" box) where children's rules apply
Tracking asked through the phone's own prompt, before any tracking (iPhone)
Button says what it does: "Create account"
Loading state; cannot be pressed twice
Button stays above the keyboard
A disabled button says why, or it stays enabled and shows the errors
Robot check only when needed, invisible first
Limits on repeated tries and code sends
Product usable before the email is confirmed
Code fills itself from the SMS (iPhone one-time-code; Android SMS Retriever or WebOTP)
Code boxes take a pasted code, move on by themselves and send on the last digit
Resend with a countdown, plus "change email or number"
"Open mail app" button on the check-your-email screen
Expired code or link: clear message and one tap for a new one
Welcome screen pointing to the first action
Signed in straight away, never "now log in"
Permissions asked when each is needed, a reason screen first, no reward for saying yes
Profile setup optional and skippable
Already-have-an-account link
Delete account inside the app (iPhone and Android) plus a web link (Android)
Touch targets at least 24 px (WCAG AA); 44 recommended, and Apple's own guide uses 44 points
Every field has a name screen readers say
Contrast passes in light and dark
Large text setting does not break the layout
Right-to-left for Arabic, with phone numbers and codes kept left-to-right
Main actions within thumb reach
Leaving halfway keeps what was typed
Invite link kept through the whole flow; returns to where they were
Works on slow mobile data

title: Splash Screen
about: What shows while the app starts, until its first screen is ready.

items.t: iOS: the launch screen looks like the first screen without content, not a branded ad
Android 12 and later: the system splash screen (icon on a colour) is shown for every app
Use the platform's splash tools; do not add a second splash screen after it
Only the app icon or logo on a plain background
No text that needs translating, no ads, no "Loading" messages
Background colour matches the first screen, in light and dark mode
Shown as briefly as possible; start-up work moved to after the first screen
Kept up only while truly needed data loads, then hand off smoothly
The first screen comes back to where the person left off
Slow start-ups measured and fixed (cold start under about 2 seconds is a good aim)
Optional short icon animation (under a second)
Reduced motion respected
Offline at start: show the app with cached content and a notice, not a stuck splash
Update required: a clear screen with a button to the store

title: Tab Bar Navigation
about: The bar at the bottom of a phone app with the main sections (also called a bottom navigation bar or dock).

items.t: 3 to 5 tabs for the main top-level sections
Each tab an icon and a short label, always shown
Labels one word where possible
Tabs are places, not actions (no "New post" tab unless it is a clear exception)
"More" tab only if really needed
Selected tab clear by filled icon, colour and label, not colour alone
Badges for counts on tabs
Bar sits above the home indicator safe area
Visible on all top-level screens; hidden only in full-screen tasks
Tapping a tab opens that section where the person left it
Tapping the current tab again scrolls to top or goes back to its root
No moving tabs around between screens
Each tab keeps its own navigation history
iOS: tab bar; Android: navigation bar (bottom) or rail on tablets
On tablets and large screens, a side rail or sidebar instead
Each tab has a name and says it is selected ("Home, tab, 1 of 5, selected")
Targets at least 44 pt / 48 dp
Labels stay readable with large text (bigger labels shown on long press on iOS)
Order flips for right-to-left languages

title: Upgrade (mobile)
about: Moving from free to paid, or from one plan to a higher one, inside a phone app.

items.t: Offer the upgrade when the person reaches a limit or a paid feature, saying what it unlocks
A lock icon on paid features, with a short reason on tap
Not interrupting a task in the middle
Current plan marked; higher plans with what is added
Prices with period and currency from the store
Yearly saving shown honestly
Free trial terms clear (length, price after, first charge date)
Through Apple or Google in-app purchase for digital features (with regional exceptions)
Upgrade within a subscription group takes effect at once on iOS; downgrade at renewal
Google Play replacement modes (charge now, prorate) chosen on purpose
Unlocked features available at once with a thank-you
Show what is new and where to find it
Restore purchases for other devices
Easy to close; no repeated offers right after "No thanks"
Downgrade and cancel explained in settings
Price and plan names read clearly
Large text supported; buttons at least 44 pt / 48 dp

title: Adding to cart (flow)
about: From choosing a product's options to the item being in the cart, with clear feedback.

items.t: Required options (size, colour) chosen first; the button says what is missing
Price, stock and delivery estimate visible near the button
Out of stock: button replaced by "Notify me", not hidden
Quantity choice where it makes sense
Button shows busy state; no double add on double tap
Works without signing in (guest cart)
Confirmation without leaving the page: a small panel or message with the item, "View cart" and "Checkout"
Cart count updates at once
Message announced to screen readers
Haptic on phones
Failure explained ("Only 2 left") with a way forward
Price changed since the page loaded: say so
Person stays where they were to keep shopping
Cart kept across visits and devices
Option pickers are real buttons or radios with names
Focus stays sensible after adding
Targets at least 24 px web / 44 pt iOS / 48 dp Android

title: Booking a time (flow)
about: Choosing a date and time slot for an appointment or meeting.

items.t: Available days and times only, in the person's time zone, shown clearly
Time zone changeable
Date picker that works by keyboard
Only the fields needed
Summary before confirming: what, when, where, price
Slot held while finishing, with a clear time limit that can be extended
Confirmation page and email with a calendar file
Reschedule and cancel links in the email
Reminders before the time
Slots announced with full date and time

title: Canceling subscription (flow)
about: Stopping a paid plan, from finding the option to confirmation.

items.t: "Cancel subscription" easy to find in billing or account settings
Cancel online if you could sign up online; no phone call required
In store-bought plans, link to the store's subscription page
As few steps as signing up
One optional offer (pause, cheaper plan, discount) is fine; repeated offers or guilt wording are not
Optional short "why are you leaving" with skip
Buttons say what they do ("Cancel subscription", "Keep my plan"), neither hidden
Access until the end of the paid period, with the date
What is lost and whether data is kept, and for how long
Refund rules if any
Confirmation screen and email with the end date
Easy way to come back (resubscribe)

EU and UK consumer rules also require easy cancelling
Every step works by keyboard and screen reader
No timed offers that pressure

title: Changing email (flow)
about: Switching the email address an account signs in with.

items.t: Current password or fresh sign-in required
The new address entered with checks
A link or code sent to the new address; the change only applies after it
A notice sent to the old address with a way to undo
Sessions on other devices reviewed
Marketing consent carried over only when right
Address already used: say so without leaking other accounts
Status announced on each step

title: Changing plan (flow)
about: Upgrading or downgrading a subscription.

items.t: Plans compared side by side, current plan marked
The new price, when it starts and any prorated charge shown before confirming
What will be lost said plainly
Data kept or exportable
One clear button naming the action
Confirmation page and email with the new terms
Plan changes for store purchases go through the store
Plan change confirmed by the payment provider before access changes

title: Contacting support (flow)
about: Getting help from a person or a bot, from the first question to an answer.

items.t: Help link in the same place on every page
Search help articles first, but never hide the way to a person
Ways shown with response times (chat now, email in 24 hours)
Choose a topic, then a short form
Account details and the page they came from attached automatically, with notice
Attach screenshots
Suggested articles as they type, without blocking sending
Bot says it is a bot
"Talk to a person" always available
Chat history kept, transcript by email
Works when the person leaves and comes back
Confirmation with a ticket number and when to expect a reply
Replies by email and in the app, threaded
Status of open requests
Rating after it is solved, short and optional
Chat works with screen readers and keyboard; new messages announced
Phone not the only way
No time-outs that lose a typed message

title: Deleting account (flow)
about: Permanently removing an account and its data, by the person's own choice.

items.t: In account settings, clearly named
Inside the app if accounts are made in the app (App Store); a web page too (Google Play)
Say what will be deleted, what is kept by law and for how long
Offer to download data first
Active subscriptions: say they must be cancelled, with a link (store plans in the store)

Password or a fresh sign-in
Typed confirmation for big accounts ("type DELETE")

Grace period to undo (for example 30 days) said clearly, with how to undo
Data deleted from all systems and backups within a stated time
Third parties told to delete
GDPR right to erasure; Saudi PDPL also gives the right to destruction of personal data
Every step works by keyboard and screen reader
No time limit on the confirmation

title: Entering promo code (flow)
about: Typing a discount code in cart or checkout and seeing the price change.

items.t: Folded behind a quiet link ("Have a code?") so people without one are not sent away to hunt for codes
Field with Apply button; Enter applies too
Not case-sensitive; spaces trimmed
Paste works
Busy state on Apply
Success: code shown as a removable tag with the saving
Totals update at once, discount on its own line

Field keeps the typed code for fixing
Too many tries slowed down
Only one code or several: say so
Codes applied in the store's price rules on the server, not only the page
Discount shown honestly against the real earlier price
Result announced
Field has a visible name
Remove button named ("Remove code SAVE10")

title: Exporting data (flow)
about: Downloading a copy of your data.

items.t: Choose what to export and the format
Personal data export available to every person

Count of results per option

A link option, with expiry

Results announced; errors linked to fields

Saved cards only with consent, shown by brand and last 4
Fields have visible names
Errors announced and linked to fields
The bank page in the check is reachable by keyboard

title: Requesting a refund (flow)
about: Asking for money back on an order or subscription.

items.t: From the order or billing page, clearly named
Pick the items and a reason
The refund amount and method shown before sending
EU 14-day withdrawal right honoured where it applies
Confirmation with a reference number and the time it takes
Refund through the original payment method
Store purchases go through the store's refund process
No hidden steps or obstacles
Errors and results announced

title: Resetting password (flow)

items.t: "Forgot password?" next to the password field
Email field filled with what was typed on login
Same message whether or not the account exists ("If an account exists, we sent a link")
Random, single use, expires soon (about an hour or less)
Sent by email, or code by SMS where that is how people sign in
Resend after a short wait
Link opens on any device
One field with Show, not two to match
Rules shown up front, checked as typed: at least 8 characters (15 if password-only), no forced mix of symbols

Password managers can fill and save (autocomplete new-password)
Signed in, or sent to login with a success message
Other sessions signed out, with the choice shown
Email telling the person the password changed, with "This wasn't me"
Requests rate-limited
Two-step check still asked if it was on
No security questions
Fields named; no time pressure
Copy-paste allowed

title: Saving changes (flow)
about: Keeping edits to a form, document or settings, by a Save button or automatically.

items.t: Autosave for documents and long writing; Save button for forms with checks
Toggles and single choices take effect at once
Don't mix both ways on one screen

Keyboard shortcut (Ctrl+S) where people expect it

title: Setting up two-step sign-in (flow)
about: Adding a second factor like an authenticator app, passkey or SMS code.

items.t: Options listed: passkey, authenticator app, then SMS as a fallback
QR code plus a text key to type

The person confirms they saved them
Email confirmation that two-step is on

title: Sharing a link (flow)

items.t: System share sheet on phones
Copy link button with a confirmation
Link previews look right (title, image, description)
Clear who can open it
Private items ask before making a public link
Short, readable and lasting
Opens the right screen in the app or on the web

Near the field, under it, tied to it for screen readers (aria-describedby)
Red border plus an icon and text, not colour alone

Layout does not jump much when the message appears
Summary at the top listing errors as links to each field
Focus moves to the summary or the first wrong field
Page title starts with "Error:" on full page forms
Everything typed is kept
Accept many formats (spaces in card numbers, +966 or 05)
Hints before typing for format rules
Right keyboard and autofill
Field marked invalid (aria-invalid)
Errors announced
Arabic and English messages in the right direction

All fields checked; error summary at the top with links

Busy state on the button; no double send

Confirmation page or message saying what happens next and when
Reference number and email copy where useful

Spam protection without robot puzzles that block people (honeypot, rate limits)

Enter submits from a text field
Result announced
Works without a mouse

A bin or history for later undo

items.t: Say why it is needed, what is collected and how long it is kept

Status shown (checking, approved, needs more) with notifications
Another way for people who cannot use the camera
Clear success and the next step

title: API authentication
about: How programs and apps prove who they are when they call an API.

Short-lived access tokens; refresh tokens that change on each use

Browser apps use Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite cookies, not tokens kept in page storage
CORS allows only your own sites, never "*" with credentials

title: API docs
about: The documentation developers read to start using an API and to fix problems.

items.t: Four kinds kept apart: a getting-started tutorial, how-to guides, the reference, and explanations
A quick start that reaches a first working call in minutes
The reference generated from the OpenAPI file so it never drifts from the code
Every address with its method, fields, types, required marks, example request and response
Every error code with its meaning and fix
Authentication, paging, rate limits and versioning explained once and linked from each address
Copyable examples in curl and the main languages, with test keys filled in for signed-in readers
Examples that are run in tests so they keep working
A changelog with dates and what callers must do
Deprecated items marked with their retire date
Search across all pages
A status page and a support contact linked from the docs
Docs pages meet WCAG: headings, keyboard use, contrast, readable code blocks

title: API errors
about: What an API sends back when something goes wrong, so both a program and a person can act on it.

items.t: One error format for the whole API, such as Problem Details (type, title, status, detail)
A stable machine code per error ("card_declined") that never changes
A human message in plain words that says what to do next
Field errors list each field and its problem, so a form can show them in place
A request id in every response and every error, also written to the logs
The status code matches the error: 4xx for the caller, 5xx for the server
401 means not signed in; 403 means signed in but not allowed
404 instead of 403 where saying "it exists" would leak information
429 and 503 carry a Retry-After header
No stack traces, database errors, file paths or library versions in responses
The same message for "wrong password" and "no such user"
Unexpected errors caught in one place, logged in detail, answered with a general message
Each error says whether trying again can help
Every error code listed in the docs with its cause and fix
Messages in the caller's language when the API serves people directly

title: API pagination
about: Returning long lists in pages so neither the server nor the caller has to handle everything at once.

items.t: Cursor paging (a next-page token) for lists that change or grow; numbered pages only for small, stable lists
The token is opaque: callers pass it back and never build it themselves
A stable sort with a unique tie-breaker (created time, then id), so nothing is skipped or shown twice
The same filters must come with each next page; changed filters are refused
A default page size and a maximum; larger requests are cut to the maximum
No "give me everything" option on big tables
A next-page token, empty on the last page
Optionally a Link header with next and previous addresses
Total count only when it is cheap; otherwise only "has more"
An expired token gives a clear error, not an empty page
Every list reads through an index that matches its sort, never a full table scan
Deep numbered pages avoided: they get slower the further you go
Paging explained once and identical on every list

title: API rate limits
about: Capping how much one caller can ask for, so one heavy user cannot slow or break the service for everyone.

items.t: Limits per key or per user, and a lower one per network address for anonymous calls
Stricter limits on costly or sensitive actions: sign-in, password reset, search, exports, AI calls
Size limits too: body size, page size, file size, query depth
A timeout on every request, so slow work cannot pile up
429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After
Headers with the limit, what is left and when it resets
Limits listed in the docs for each plan
Counted in one shared store, so all servers agree
Smooth counting (a sliding window or token bucket) so bursts cannot slip through at each reset
Under overload, the least important work is dropped first and core actions keep working
Callers told to retry with growing waits and a random spread
Anything that costs money per call (AI, SMS, email, maps) has a daily cap in code
An alert when one caller or the whole service nears its cap
Repeated hits on a limit are logged and reviewed

title: API versioning
about: Changing an API without breaking the programs that already use it.

items.t: Removing or renaming a field, an address or an error code
Changing a field's type, format or meaning
Making an optional input required
Adding fields or enum values is safe only if clients were told to ignore unknown ones
One version scheme for the whole API: in the path (/v1), a header or a dated version
Each account pinned to the version it started on; it upgrades by choice
Old versions translated at the edge, so the core code has one model
Deprecation and Sunset headers with the date on anything being retired
Notice sent well ahead (often 6 to 12 months) by email and in the changelog
Use of old versions measured, so you know who to contact
Every change listed with its date, version and what callers must do
Breaking changes clearly marked
Contract tests prove old versions still answer as documented
The OpenAPI file is compared on every change to catch breaking ones
Changes rolled out in steps: add the new, move callers, then remove the old

title: File uploads (API)
about: Accepting files through an API without letting them harm the server or other users.

items.t: Allowed file types listed; checked by content, not only by name
Size limit per file and per account, told to the caller up front
Large files go straight to storage through a short-lived signed address
Files renamed with random names; the original name kept only as text
Stored outside the web root, served from a separate domain
Images re-encoded to strip hidden content and location data
Virus scan before the file is shared with anyone
Archives unpacked only with limits on size and file count
Download links that expire and check permission
Content-Disposition attachment and nosniff on downloads
Resumable uploads for big files, with progress
Clear errors for wrong type, too big or failed scan
Uploads never finished are removed after a set time

title: GraphQL API
about: An API where the caller writes a query naming exactly the data it wants.

items.t: One schema with clear type and field names, descriptions on every type and field
Nullable fields by default where parts can fail; required only when always present
Changes are added rather than versioned; old fields marked @deprecated with a reason
Connection-style paging (edges, cursors, pageInfo) with a maximum page size
Query depth and cost limited, so one query cannot ask for millions of rows
Introspection and the query explorer switched off for the public in production, unless the API is public by design
Authorization checked in every field resolver or the data layer, not only at the top
Batching and aliases limited, so they cannot be used to guess passwords
Inputs validated like any API; errors without internal details
Data loaded in batches to avoid one database call per item
Known queries can be stored and called by id (persisted queries)
Errors in the errors list with a stable code in extensions
Limits based on query cost, not only on the number of calls

title: Idempotency and retries
about: Making it safe to send the same request twice, so a dropped connection never charges a card twice.

items.t: Actions that create (payments, orders, messages) accept an idempotency key from the caller
The same key with the same body returns the first result without doing the work again
The same key with a different body is refused with a clear error
Keys kept for at least 24 hours
The key and the result saved in the same transaction as the work
Two requests with the same key at the same moment: one waits or gets 409, never both run
A database uniqueness rule as the last guard (one payment per order)
Clients retry only safe or idempotent requests
Growing waits with a random spread and a maximum number of tries
Retry only on errors that can pass (timeouts, 429, 503), never on 400
A timeout at every layer, each shorter than the layer calling it
A circuit breaker stops calling a service that keeps failing
Consumers handle the same message twice safely by remembering processed ids
Events written in the same transaction as the change (an outbox table), then sent

title: Realtime connections
about: Pushing live updates to apps over WebSockets or server-sent events.

items.t: Server-sent events when only the server talks; WebSockets when both sides send
Polling only when updates are rare, and then slowly
Secure connections only (wss)
The Origin header checked when the connection opens
The user signed in when connecting, and checked again for each private channel
Every incoming message validated and size-limited
Heartbeats close dead connections
Clients reconnect with growing waits and a random spread
After reconnecting, the client catches up from its last event id
Limits on connections per user and messages per second
One message format with a type and an id
Missed messages are not assumed delivered; important state is also readable from the normal API
Fan-out through a shared message service so any server can reach any client
Data that changes every few seconds is batched or sent as a summary

title: Receiving webhooks
about: Accepting event calls from another service safely, without double work or lost events.

items.t: Signature checked against the raw body before anything else
Timestamp checked; messages older than about 5 minutes are refused (no replays)
Secrets kept in the secret store, never in code
Answer 2xx fast, then do the work in a background job
Each event id stored; a repeat is acknowledged and skipped
Events may arrive out of order: compare times or fetch the latest state before acting
Only the event types you need are handled; others are acknowledged and ignored
Failed processing retried from your own queue, not by failing the call
A daily check against the sender's API catches events that never arrived
Alerts when deliveries stop or errors rise
App Store and Google Play subscription events handled the same way (signed, recorded, deduplicated)
Tested with the sender's test events and command-line tools before going live

title: REST API design
about: The shape of an HTTP API: addresses, methods, bodies and status codes that other programs rely on.

items.t: Nouns for resources (/orders/123), plural collections, no verbs in the path
Lowercase paths with hyphens, and one naming style for fields used everywhere
Identifiers that cannot be guessed (random or time-ordered UUIDs), not running numbers
Nesting at most one level deep (/orders/123/items)
GET only reads and is safe to repeat
POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes some fields, DELETE removes
PUT and DELETE give the same result when repeated
Actions that are not create, read, change or delete get their own sub-address with POST (/orders/123:cancel)
JSON with a declared content type; dates as RFC 3339 text with a time zone
Money as an amount in the smallest unit plus a currency code (24500 and "SAR")
Only fields a caller may set are accepted; unknown or protected fields are refused
Responses never include fields the caller may not see (password hashes, other customers)
200 done, 201 created with a Location header, 204 done with nothing to return
400 bad input, 401 not signed in, 403 not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 checks failed
5xx only for the server's own failures, never for the caller's mistakes
Lists are paged from the first version
Callers can ask for only the fields they need
ETag on reads so a client can ask "changed since?" and get 304 Not Modified
The whole API described in an OpenAPI file kept in step with the code
Security reviewed against the OWASP API Top 10 before launch

title: Sending webhooks
about: Telling other systems when something happens, by calling an address they gave you.

items.t: One envelope for every event: id, type, time, and the data or a link to it
Event types named object.action (invoice.paid) and listed in the docs
Small payloads; the receiver fetches full details when needed
Every message signed with a secret per endpoint and a timestamp
Secrets can be rotated with two valid at once during the switch
Only HTTPS addresses accepted; private and internal addresses blocked
Retries with growing waits for about 3 days; a 2xx answer means delivered
Short timeout per attempt (for example 10 to 15 seconds)
Order is not promised; each event carries its time so receivers can sort
An endpoint failing for days is switched off and its owner emailed
Each endpoint picks which events it wants
A delivery log with each attempt, its status and the answer
Buttons to send a test event and to re-send a failed one
Events also readable through an API list, so missed ones can be fetched

title: AI features (server)
about: Building features on language models safely, within budget, and honestly.

items.t: Prompt injection planned for: model output never trusted to take actions alone
Model output checked and encoded before showing or using it
No secrets or other users' data in prompts
Tools the model can call are limited, and risky ones need a person's yes
A daily cap per user and in total, counted in one place
Repeated answers cached
Input and output size limited
A test set of real questions run before each model or prompt change
Answers that state when they are unsure; sources shown where possible
People told when they are talking to an AI or seeing AI content
A way to report a bad answer
What is sent to the model provider is stated in the privacy notice
Provider settings checked so your data is not used for their training without consent

title: Audit trail
about: A permanent record of who did what, for security, support and the law.

items.t: Sign-ins, permission changes, data exports, deletes and admin actions recorded
Each entry: who, what, which record, when, from where, and the result
Before and after values for important changes
Entries cannot be changed or deleted by the app
Stored apart from normal data, with its own access rules
Times in UTC from a synced clock
No passwords, tokens or full card numbers in entries
Kept for a stated period, then removed
Customers can see their own account's trail where it helps
Searchable by user, record and time
Alerts on suspicious patterns

title: Authentication (server)
about: How the server checks who someone is: passwords, codes, passkeys and sign-in limits.

items.t: At least 8 characters (15 when it is the only factor), up to at least 64, all characters allowed
Checked against lists of leaked and common passwords
No forced rules about symbols and no forced regular changes
Stored with a slow, salted hash (Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt)
Passkeys offered where supported
A second factor available, required for admins
One-time codes expire quickly, work once and are limited in tries
Sign in with Apple or Google through standard OAuth with PKCE
Attempts limited per account and per network address, with growing delays
The same answer whether or not the account exists
Password reset links random, single-use and short-lived
Sign-ins, failures, resets and factor changes logged without the secrets
The user told by email about a new device or a changed password
The design checked against OWASP ASVS level 2

title: Authorization
about: Deciding what each signed-in person may see and do, checked on the server every time.

items.t: Deny by default; access granted only by explicit rules
Roles or permissions defined in one place, not scattered through the code
Least privilege: each role gets only what its job needs
Checked on the server for every action, never only by hiding buttons
Object-level checks: the record must belong to the caller (no reading order 124 by changing the number)
Field-level checks: some fields only some roles may read or change
Admin actions behind separate checks and, ideally, a separate address
Row-level security as a second guard for shared tables
The app's database user cannot change the schema
Role changes take effect immediately
Every grant, removal and admin action written to the audit trail
Tests that try each action as each role, including "should be refused" cases

title: Background jobs
about: Work done outside the request (emails, exports, processing), safely and in order.

items.t: A queue that keeps jobs if a server restarts
Each job safe to run twice (idempotent)
Jobs created in the same transaction as the change that needs them (outbox)
A timeout per job
Retries with growing waits, a maximum number of tries, then a dead-letter list
Limits on how many jobs run at once, per kind and per customer
Jobs start when there is work, not on a busy timer
Progress saved so a restart continues instead of starting over
A status the person can see (queued, running, done, failed) with a result link
Queue length, age of the oldest job and failure rate measured with alerts
Each job logged with its id, tries and result
Jobs run with only the rights they need

title: Caching
about: Keeping copies of answers so repeated requests are fast and cheap, without serving wrong data.

items.t: Cache-Control on every response: public, private or no-store
Personal pages marked private or no-store
ETag or Last-Modified so clients can ask "changed since?"
Static files with content hashes in their names, cached for a year
Cache keys include everything that changes the answer (user, language, tenant)
A time limit on every cached item
Clear invalidation when the source changes
Protection against many requests rebuilding the same item at once
Never cache answers with another user's data under a shared key
The app still works when the cache is empty or down
Expensive results (AI answers, outside lookups) cached
Hit rate and size measured

title: Concurrency
about: Keeping data right when many people or servers change the same thing at once.

items.t: Optimistic locking: a version or ETag must match, or the change is refused
Database locks for counters and stock, taken in a fixed order to avoid deadlocks
Isolation levels chosen for money and stock moves
Unique rules prevent double creates
Busy counters split across several rows and added up when read
Conflicts and retries measured as a warning sign
Transactions that fail on conflict retried a few times with a wait
Side effects (emails, payments) happen after the transaction commits, via an outbox
Every message handler is idempotent
Tests that run the same action in parallel

title: Data privacy (server)
about: Handling personal data the way GDPR and Saudi PDPL require.

items.t: A list of what personal data is kept, why, where and for how long
A legal reason for each use
Collect only what is needed
Privacy built into the design from the start
Access and a copy of their data
Correction and deletion, including from backups within a stated time
Objection to marketing and profiling
Encryption in transit and at rest, access limited by role
Breaches reported within 72 hours where required
A data processing agreement with each supplier
Transfers outside the country only under the rules
An impact assessment for high-risk processing
Saudi cybersecurity controls checked where they apply

title: Database design
about: Tables, keys and rules that keep data correct and fast as it grows.

items.t: One table per kind of thing; no lists hidden inside text columns
Primary keys on every table; random or time-ordered ids for public ones
Foreign keys between related tables
NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK rules for what must always be true
Times stored as UTC timestamps with time zone
Money as whole numbers in the smallest unit, or exact decimals, never floating point
Fixed lists as enums or lookup tables
Indexes on columns used to filter, join or sort
Slow queries checked with EXPLAIN before release
Lists always paged; no unbounded reads
Steps that must happen together run in one transaction
The right isolation level for money and stock
Personal data in clearly marked columns, so it can be exported and deleted
Sensitive columns encrypted
Each customer's rows marked by tenant and guarded by row rules

title: Database migrations
about: Changing the database structure safely while the app keeps running.

items.t: Every change as a numbered migration file kept with the code
Migrations run automatically in each environment, in order, once
Tested on a copy of real-sized data before production
Change in steps: add the new, write to both, move readers, then remove the old
New columns start nullable or with a default
Indexes built without locking the table (CONCURRENTLY)
Long locks avoided; a lock timeout set for migration runs
Big data changes in batches, not in one transaction
A backup or restore point before risky changes
A way back written for each step, or a plan to fix forward
No destructive change (drop, rename) in the same release as the code that stops using it
The schema version is visible and logged

title: Dates, times and money
about: Storing and showing times, currencies and numbers correctly for every country.

items.t: Stored in UTC; shown in the person's time zone
Time zones by name (Asia/Riyadh), not by fixed offset
Text dates in RFC 3339 or ISO 8601
Hijri and Gregorian calendars shown where people expect them
Daylight saving handled for countries that use it
Whole numbers in the smallest unit or exact decimals, never floating point
The currency code stored with every amount
Rounding rules stated and applied once
Exchange rates stored with the time they were used
Numbers, dates and currency formatted by locale (Intl)
Arabic-Indic or Western digits by the person's choice
Tests at month ends, leap years and time-zone changes

title: Email sending
about: Sending account and product emails that arrive in the inbox and follow the law.

items.t: SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up for the sending domain
Gmail and Yahoo rules met: alignment, low spam rate, one-click unsubscribe for bulk mail
Account emails and marketing emails sent from separate addresses or streams
A plain-text version with every HTML email
The sender's name and postal address in marketing emails
Marketing only with consent where the law needs it
One-click unsubscribe header and a working link, honoured quickly
Sending through a queue with retries
Bounces and complaints handled: stop sending to bad addresses
Daily caps per user and in total
No secrets or full card numbers in emails
Links in emails expire when they sign someone in
Delivery, bounce and complaint rates measured

title: Feature flags
about: Switching features on and off without a new release.

items.t: Flags for gradual rollouts, quick switch-offs, experiments and plan features
One flag service or library (such as OpenFeature) instead of scattered checks
Rolled out by percentage or group, with the same user always in the same group
A kill switch for any risky feature
Rollouts watched for errors before going wider
Flags checked on the server for anything that controls access or money
A safe default when the flag service is down
Every flag has an owner and an end date
Old flags removed from the code once fully on
Flag changes logged with who and when

title: File storage
about: Keeping uploaded and generated files safe, private and affordable.

items.t: Files in object storage, not in the database or on one server's disk
Private by default; shared only through expiring signed links
Encrypted at rest
Type and size checked, files renamed, scanned before sharing
Image metadata (like location) removed
Served from a separate domain with safe headers
Thumbnails and sizes made once and cached
Old and unfinished uploads cleaned up by rule
Files deleted when their owner deletes them, including copies
Backups of important files, tested
Storage and transfer measured against the plan's limits

title: Input validation
about: Checking everything that comes in before the server uses it.

items.t: Checked on the server even when the screen checks too
Checked as early as possible, at the edge of the system
Allow-lists: say what is allowed (type, length, range, pattern), not what is banned
A schema for every request body; unknown fields refused
Text normalised (Unicode NFC) before comparing or storing
Sizes capped: body, strings, arrays, file sizes
Database queries always use parameters, never joined strings
Output encoded for where it goes (HTML, address, JSON)
No user input in shell commands or file paths
Addresses supplied by users fetched only through an allow-list (no internal addresses)
No reading of untrusted serialised objects
Redirects only to known addresses
Clear field errors to the caller, without internal details

title: Multi-tenancy
about: Keeping many customers in one system without any of them seeing another.

items.t: Every row carries its tenant id
Every query filtered by tenant, ideally forced by row-level security
The tenant comes from the signed-in session, never from a field the caller sends
Files and cache keys include the tenant
Limits per tenant so one cannot slow the others
Heavy jobs queued per tenant
Staff access to a tenant is granted, time-limited and logged
Export and delete of a whole tenant
A tenant can be restored without restoring everyone
Tests that try to read and change another tenant's data and must fail

title: Notification delivery
about: Getting push, email and in-app messages to the right person once, at the right time.

items.t: Push through FCM and APNs with tokens kept per device
Dead device tokens removed when the service reports them
Each person's channel choices stored and respected
One place decides what to send on which channel
Sent from a queue with retries; never twice for one event
Quiet hours and the person's time zone respected
Similar messages grouped instead of many in a row
No private details on lock-screen text unless the person allows it
A link that opens the right screen
Caps per person per day
SMS and email counted against daily budgets
Delivery, open and failure rates measured

title: Payments (server)
about: Taking money safely: payment intents, webhooks, refunds and records.

items.t: Card details collected by the payment provider; your servers never see them
Card fields hosted by the provider keep you at the lightest PCI level
One payment intent per order, created on the server with the amount set by the server
An idempotency key on every create call
Bank checks (3-D Secure) handled where required
The order marked paid only from a signed webhook, not from the browser
Amounts as whole numbers in the smallest unit with a currency code
VAT added and shown correctly; e-invoices where required
Refunds through the provider, linked to the original payment
Disputes tracked with evidence and deadlines
Store subscriptions checked on the server with the store's notifications
A ledger of every charge, refund and fee, matched to the provider each day
Logs never contain card numbers or full bank details

title: Scheduled jobs
about: Work that runs at set times, like reminders, reports and clean-ups.

items.t: Times kept in UTC; local times turned into UTC with the time-zone database
Daylight-saving gaps and repeats handled for local schedules
Runs no more often than the data really changes
A lock so only one server runs each job
Safe to run twice and safe to skip a run
Missed runs (server down) caught up or skipped by a clear rule
Work done in batches with limits, not all at once
Large jobs spread over time so they do not overload the database
Each run logged with its start, end and result
An alert when a job fails or does not run at all
Copies in test and dev run less often, or not at all

title: Search (server)
about: Finding records by words quickly and fairly.

items.t: A full-text index rather than LIKE scans
Arabic and English handled: language rules, letter forms and diacritics
The index updated when records change
Typos forgiven where possible
Results ranked by match and then by freshness or popularity
Filters use indexes too
Results paged with a maximum
Each person sees only results they may open
Query length and complexity limited
Search input passed as a parameter, never joined into a query
Searches with no results logged to improve the index
Slow searches measured

title: Sessions
about: Keeping a person signed in safely between requests.

items.t: A long random id made by the server
Sent in a cookie marked Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite
A new id after sign-in and after any change in rights
An idle timeout and an absolute timeout, shorter for sensitive apps
Sign-out ends the session on the server, not only in the browser
"Sign out everywhere" and a list of active devices
Password change ends all other sessions
Forms that change things protected against cross-site requests (SameSite plus tokens)
Sensitive actions ask for the password again
Session data stored server-side; nothing secret in the cookie
Phone apps keep tokens in the system's secure storage
Refresh tokens change on each use; reuse of an old one ends the session
Session starts and ends logged with device and place

title: Backups
about: Copies of data you can actually restore when something goes wrong.

items.t: How much data you can lose (RPO) and how long you can be down (RTO) agreed
Point-in-time recovery for the main database
3 copies, on 2 kinds of storage, 1 in another place
Backups encrypted
At least one copy cannot be changed or deleted by the app's accounts
Access to backups limited and logged
Restores tested on a schedule, timed, and written up
A full disaster-recovery practice at least yearly
Files, settings and secrets covered, not only the database
Deleted personal data removed from backups within a stated time
An alert when a backup fails or is late

title: Cost and usage limits
about: Making every paid service last its whole billing period and never surprise you with a bill.

items.t: Each paid service listed with its plan, limits, reset date and which copies share them
A daily budget per service (limit divided by days)
Code that spends per call (AI, SMS, email, maps) counts use and stops at a daily cap
Retries give up after a few tries
Spending alerts and hard caps set in each provider's console
Jobs start when there is work, not on fast timers
Test and dev copies use cheaper or separate accounts
Repeated lookups and AI answers cached
Unused servers, files and copies removed
Usage compared with the pace line each week; alerts at 50% and 80% when ahead of pace

title: Dependencies
about: The outside code your app is built on, kept up to date and trustworthy.

items.t: A list of every dependency and its version (a lock file and a software bill of materials)
Licences checked before adding
Prefer maintained, widely used packages; check their health score
Fewer dependencies where a small amount of own code will do
Automatic alerts for known vulnerabilities
Updates applied regularly in small steps, with tests
Critical fixes applied within days
Packages installed from trusted sources with locked versions and checks
Build steps signed or verified

title: Deployment
about: Putting new versions live safely and often, with a quick way back.

items.t: Every change goes through the same automatic build, test and release steps
Builds are repeatable and produce one package used in every environment
Settings come from the environment, not from code
Small, frequent releases
Canary or gradual rollouts, watched before going wider
One click or command to roll back
Database changes made compatible with old and new code
Health checks before traffic reaches a new version
Release notes and the version number visible
Pipeline secrets kept in the secret store; steps run with least privilege
Only reviewed changes to main can deploy
Deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate and time to restore tracked

title: Environments
about: The separate copies of the system (dev, test, production) and how they are kept apart.

items.t: Dev, test and production in separate accounts or projects
No production data in dev or test; fake or masked data instead
Different secrets and keys in each
The same build runs in every environment; only settings differ
Infrastructure described as code
Production access limited to few people, logged, and time-limited
Test copies not open to the public, or protected by sign-in
Test copies scaled down or switched off when not used
The environment name shown clearly in each copy

title: Incident response
about: What happens when the service breaks: who leads, how people are told, and how it gets learned from.

items.t: Who is on call is written, with a backup
Runbooks for the common failures
Severity levels defined with examples
One incident lead; roles for talking, fixing and writing down
Stop the harm first, find the cause later
A running timeline of what was done
Customers told on the status page early and updated regularly
Personal data breaches reported to the authority within 72 hours where required
Affected people told when the risk is high
A blameless postmortem with causes and actions
Actions have owners and dates, and are followed up
Lessons shared with the whole team

title: Logging
about: Writing down what the system does, so problems can be found and explained.

items.t: Structured logs (JSON) with time, level, message, service and request id
One request id carried through every service and job
Times in UTC
Errors with enough detail to fix them
Security events: sign-ins, failures, permission changes, admin actions
Each request: route, status, time taken
No passwords, tokens, keys, card numbers or full personal data
User input cleaned before logging so it cannot fake log lines
Logs sent to one central place, not left on servers
Kept for a stated time, then removed
Access to logs limited and itself logged
Log levels set so production is not flooded; noisy logs sampled

title: Monitoring and alerts
about: Knowing the service is healthy, and waking someone only when people are affected.

items.t: The four golden signals: traffic, errors, time taken and how full the system is
Service level objectives (for example 99.9% of requests succeed) agreed and written
Checks from outside that act like a user (synthetic checks)
Alert on user pain (SLO burn rate), not on every high number
Every alert can be acted on and links to a runbook
Urgent alerts page someone; the rest go to a ticket
Noisy alerts fixed or removed
One overview page per service
Traces across services
A public status page during problems
Usage of paid services watched against limits, with alerts at 50% and 80%

title: Performance
about: Keeping the service fast as use grows, and knowing what fast means.

items.t: Speed targets per action (for example 95% of searches under 300 ms)
Web pages meet Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS)
Slow database queries found and fixed with EXPLAIN
Indexes for every common filter and sort
Caching for repeated reads
No one-call-per-item loops to the database
Load tests before big launches, on a separate copy
Timeouts and limits so overload slows things down instead of breaking them
Failures in one part do not spread to others
Time taken measured per route at the 50th, 95th and 99th percentile
Real users' speed measured, not only lab tests

title: Secrets
about: Keeping passwords, keys and tokens out of code and out of the wrong hands.

items.t: Secrets in a secret store or environment settings, never in code or git
Secret scanning on every push; leaks revoked at once
Separate secrets for dev, test and production
Each service gets only the secrets it needs
Access to secrets logged
Secrets rotated on a schedule and after anyone leaves
Rotation without downtime (two valid during the switch)
Short-lived credentials where the platform offers them
Secrets never printed in logs, errors or build output
Shared with people only through the secret store, never by chat or email

title: Security headers
about: The settings a web server sends that tell browsers how to protect its pages.

items.t: HTTPS everywhere, with HSTS
A Content Security Policy that allows only your own scripts
X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
Frames blocked with frame-ancestors (or X-Frame-Options) unless needed
Referrer-Policy set (strict-origin-when-cross-origin)
Permissions-Policy turns off unused features (camera, location)
Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite on session cookies
CORS allows only known sites
Server and framework version headers removed
A security.txt file says where to report problems
Headers checked automatically on each release

title: Testing
about: Automatic checks that catch mistakes before people see them.

items.t: Many small unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests
Contract tests for APIs between services
Every bug fixed gets a test that would have caught it
Permission tests for each role, including refused cases
Edge cases: empty, very long, Arabic and right-to-left text, time zones
Accessibility checks on key screens
Tests run on every change and block merging when they fail
Flaky tests fixed or removed, not ignored
Tests use their own data and clean up after themselves
No real personal data in test environments
Dependency and code scanning in the pipeline
